name: Design an E-commerce Checkout
intent: Turn a cart into exactly one paid, shipped order, without selling stock that does not exist or leaving stock locked by people who walked away, even when a hundred thousand shoppers chase a few thousand units.
codeTitle: stock reservations, an order saga and an outbox
finalIntro: One shopper buying a limited-edition phone in a flash sale.
prompt: Design the checkout of an online shop. Shoppers fill a cart and press Buy. The system has to check the stock, take the payment, create the shipment and confirm the order. On a normal day this is a few hundred orders per second, but a flash sale puts 20,000 units in front of two million shoppers in the same minute. Payment processing itself is covered in the payment system study, so focus on stock and on coordinating the steps.
functional: Keep a cart per shopper, with prices and availability checked again at checkout
Reserve stock for a shopper while they pay, and give it back if they do not
Place an order once, even if the button is pressed twice or the request is retried
Coordinate stock, payment and shipping, and undo the earlier steps when a later one fails
Tell other systems (email, warehouse, analytics) about every order change
Run flash sales on a small, fixed stock
nonFunctional: Never confirm more orders than there is stock (no overselling)
Never leave stock locked for long by shoppers who have gone away
Never charge a shopper for an order that is not confirmed, and never confirm one that was not charged
Place an order within about a second at the normal peak of a few hundred orders per second
Survive a crash of any service in the middle of an order
In a flash sale, serve millions of requests per second at the edge while the database sees only a trickle
Be fair: earlier shoppers should win over later ones

firstAttempt.text: One application and one database. Pressing Buy starts a database transaction that reads the stock, creates the order, calls the payment provider, decrements the stock and commits. Every item added to a cart immediately reduces the displayed stock, and an order confirmation email is sent at the end of the same request.
limits: Checking the stock and decrementing it later are separate steps, so concurrent buyers all see the last unit and the shop oversells
The payment call sits inside a database transaction, which holds row locks for seconds while the provider answers
A timeout after the money moved leaves a charged shopper with no order, and a retry charges them twice
If the process dies after the commit but before the email, the message is lost for good
Every shopper touches the same stock row in a flash sale, so the sale runs at the speed of one lock
Carts that reduce the stock without an expiry let abandoned carts lock the units for ever

steps.title: Keep the cart separate from the stock
steps.problem: If putting an item in the cart reduces the stock, every browsing shopper and every abandoned cart removes units that nobody has paid for, and the order flow shares a database with the cart's constant traffic.
steps.fix: The cart becomes its own service with its own key-value store, keyed by shopper, with an expiry of a few days. It holds item ids, quantities and the price the shopper saw, but it does not touch the stock. At checkout the order service reads the cart and checks it again against the catalogue: the current price, and whether the item is still available. If the price changed the shopper is asked to confirm. The cart is cheap, can lose data without harm, and scales on its own.
steps.tradeoff: Browsing never costs stock, and a cart can be rebuilt or dropped without any accounting. The price is that a cart makes no promise: the item can be gone when the shopper presses Buy, so the real promise has to be made at checkout.

steps.title: Reserve stock with a hold that expires
steps.problem: Checking the stock and decrementing it are two steps, so two shoppers can both read 1 and both buy it. The opposite fix, taking stock when the item is added to the cart and keeping it until the shopper pays, locks units for as long as the cart lives.
steps.fix: A dedicated inventory service owns the stock. Pressing Buy asks it for a reservation, which is a single conditional update such as 'set available = available - 1 where sku = 7 and available >= 1', plus a hold row with an order id and an expiry a few minutes away. The database applies the condition and the decrement together, so the stock cannot go below zero however many requests arrive at once. A repeat of the same request for the same order id finds its hold and changes nothing. When payment succeeds the hold is committed, and if the payment fails, or the shopper walks away, the hold is released, either explicitly or by a sweeper that runs when the expiry passes. The payment call happens outside the transaction.
steps.tradeoff: Overselling is impossible, and the units of people who leave come back by themselves. The expiry is a dial: a long one locks stock, so the page may say sold out while units are still held by someone who may never pay. A short one cancels slow but honest payers. A late payer has to try to take a new hold, which can fail if the stock is gone.

steps.title: Place the order once, and run it as a saga
steps.problem: The order touches three services that each have their own database, so there is no single transaction. A timeout, a crash or a double click can leave a reserved unit without an order, or a charge without a reservation, and a retry can do each step twice.
steps.fix: The checkout page gets an idempotency key when it loads, and sends it with Buy. The order service inserts the order under a unique constraint on that key, so the second request finds the first order and returns it. The order then moves through a state machine driven by a saga: reserve the stock, charge the payment (passing the order id as the payment's own idempotency key), and confirm. Each step has a compensation for the case when a later step fails: a declined card releases the hold, and a refund undoes a charge. The saga persists its state after each step, so a crashed process resumes from where it stopped.
steps.tradeoff: No distributed transaction and no locks across services, and each step can be retried safely. The system is only eventually consistent between steps: a reserved unit with no order exists for a moment, compensations must themselves be idempotent and retried until they work, and the design needs a clear order of steps, with the hardest to undo (the charge) after the easy ones.

steps.title: Write events with the order, in an outbox
steps.problem: After the order changes, shipping, email, the warehouse and analytics all need to hear about it. If the service updates its database and then publishes to a broker, a crash in between loses the event, and publishing first can announce an order that was never saved.
steps.fix: Each status change inserts an outbox row in the same database transaction as the order itself, so either both exist or neither does. A relay reads unsent rows in order and publishes them to the event bus, then marks them sent. If it crashes after publishing and before marking, the row is published again, so delivery is at least once and every consumer ignores an event id it has already applied. Shipping reacts to the 'order paid' event and reports back with an event the saga handles. If shipping cannot deliver to the address, the saga refunds the payment and puts the unit back in stock.
steps.tradeoff: No order change is ever lost or invented, and slow consumers cannot slow the checkout. Events arrive a moment late and sometimes twice, consumers need an id check, and the outbox table needs cleaning up. A step whose failure comes late, like an undeliverable address, is turned into a refund rather than a rollback.

steps.title: Protect the stock in a flash sale
steps.problem: Two million shoppers want 20,000 units in the same minute. The stock row can take roughly a thousand updates per second, so ordinary reservation turns into a pile of lock waits, timeouts and retries, and the retries are the bulk of the load.
steps.fix: A waiting room at the edge puts shoppers in a queue in order of arrival and lets in only as many as there are free units, so the number of people allowed to check out never greatly exceeds the stock. Admitted shoppers get a signed token with a short life. A hot stock counter in memory is decremented atomically before a request reaches the order service, so 'sold out' is answered at once from the counter and from the edge cache, and only the winners reach the database, which stays the source of truth through the reservations. When holds expire or payments fail, the counter is incremented and the next shopper in the queue is admitted.
steps.tradeoff: The database sees thousands of requests rather than millions, the outcome is fair by arrival order, and nobody refreshes in a fury. The price is the machinery: the counter and the database can drift apart and must be reconciled, the queue needs fair and abuse-resistant tokens (bots, many tabs), and the sold-out message is only final after the last hold has expired.

steps.title: Reconcile, expire and watch
steps.problem: Services crash halfway through sagas, counters drift from the database, and holds can stay behind. Without a check, these defects stay hidden until a shopper complains or the stock is wrong at the end of a sale.
steps.fix: A reconciler runs on a schedule. It finds orders that have been pending for too long and pushes them on or compensates them, sweeps holds past their expiry, and compares the hot counter with the stock table, correcting the counter from the database. Dashboards and alerts track the numbers that define the system: units sold above stock (must be zero), active holds, the age of the oldest pending order, outbox lag, charged-but-unconfirmed orders, and the time from open to sold out.
steps.tradeoff: Rare failures get fixed without a person, and the invariants are watched rather than hoped for. It adds another moving part, and its repairs must themselves be safe to repeat, so that two reconcilers (or a reconciler racing a live saga) cannot do harm.

failures.scenario: The shopper presses Buy twice, or the app retries after a timeout
failures.impact: Two orders could be created, two units reserved and the card charged twice.
failures.answer: Both requests carry the same idempotency key, so the unique constraint admits only one order and the second request receives it. The reservation is keyed by order id, and the charge uses the order id as its own idempotency key, so a repeat of any step changes nothing.

failures.scenario: The order service crashes after charging the card and before confirming the order
failures.impact: The shopper has paid, the stock is held, and the order is stuck in a pending state.
failures.answer: The saga stored its state before the charge, so on restart (or when the reconciler notices the old pending order) it resumes at the next step. Repeating the charge with the same key returns the first result, so nothing is charged again. If the hold expired in the meantime, the saga tries to take a new one and refunds the payment if the unit is gone.

failures.scenario: Shipping cannot deliver to the address after the payment succeeded
failures.impact: The shopper has paid for an order that will never ship.
failures.answer: The shipping service reports the failure as an event, and the saga runs its compensations in reverse order: refund the payment, put the unit back in stock, and mark the order cancelled. The unit goes back to the next shopper in the queue, and the shopper is told why.

failures.scenario: The relay crashes after publishing an event and before marking it sent
failures.impact: The event will be published again, and consumers might ship or email twice.
failures.answer: Delivery is at least once by design. Every event has a stable id, and each consumer records the ids it has applied, so a repeat is ignored. The alternative of marking the row first would lose events, which is worse.

failures.scenario: A shopper reserves the last unit, then closes the tab
failures.impact: Other shoppers see 'sold out' while the unit sits in a hold that will never be paid.
failures.answer: The hold expires after a few minutes and the unit returns to the stock. The waiting room admits the next shopper in line at that moment, and the page only calls the sale sold out once no holds remain. A shorter hold at the payment step keeps the delay small.

failures.scenario: The hot counter and the stock table disagree
failures.impact: The counter says sold out with units left (lost sales), or says available with none left (many reservations that fail).
failures.answer: The database is the truth, and the reservation's conditional update refuses any oversell even if the counter is wrong. The reconciler recomputes the counter from the stock table and the active holds, and alerts when the difference grows beyond a few units.

alternatives.title: When to take the stock

options.name: Check at the cart and decrement after payment
options.pro: Simple, and nothing is ever locked
options.con: Everyone who passes the check pays, so in a rush many more orders than units are paid for and must be refunded

options.name: Reserve when the item is added to the cart
options.pro: The shopper knows the item is theirs
options.con: Abandoned carts lock units until the expiry, so the page says sold out while stock sits idle

options.name: Atomic decrement at checkout, with a short hold
options.pro: Reserves only for shoppers who intend to pay, and gives back quickly
options.con: A shopper can fail to get the item after filling the cart

options.name: A queue in front of the stock
options.pro: Fair by arrival, no oversell, and the stock is never contended
options.con: Slower to finish, and needs a waiting room and tokens

alternatives.pick: A short hold taken at checkout for normal sales, with a queue in front for flash sales.

alternatives.title: How to coordinate the services

options.name: Orchestrated saga
options.pro: One place holds the order's flow, so it is easy to follow and to resume
options.con: The orchestrator knows every service and must be kept highly available

options.name: Choreographed events
options.pro: Services stay decoupled and react to each other's events
options.con: The flow is spread over many services, which makes it hard to see, debug and change

options.name: Two-phase commit
options.con: Holds locks across services, blocks on a failed coordinator, and is rarely supported

alternatives.pick: An orchestrated saga for the order, with events from the outbox for the consumers around it.

alternatives.title: How the stock decrement is stored

options.name: A conditional update on one row
options.pro: Simple and correct, and the database does the locking
options.con: About a thousand updates per second per hot row

options.name: Split the stock into several rows (buckets)
options.pro: Spreads the writes and the locks over many rows
options.con: A shopper can find a bucket empty while others still have units, so the buckets must be searched or rebalanced

options.name: An in-memory counter in front, with the database as the truth
options.pro: Very high rate, with an immediate sold-out answer
options.con: Two copies that can drift and need reconciling

alternatives.pick: A conditional update as the truth, with an in-memory counter in front for hot items.

alternatives.title: What to do when the stock runs out

options.name: Show sold out and stop
options.con: Shoppers do not know that held units may return

options.name: Keep a waiting list that is served as holds expire
options.pro: Every returned unit is sold, to the next person in line
options.con: More state, and notifications to send

options.name: Allow backorders
options.pro: Sells more than is on the shelf
options.con: Only valid if the shop can actually supply later

alternatives.pick: A waiting list during a flash sale, and a plain sold-out message once all holds have expired.

roles.label: Entry points
roles.description: The gateway and the waiting room that admits shoppers.

roles.label: Event bus
roles.description: Order events on their way to shipping and the saga.

roles.label: Services
roles.description: Cart, order, saga, inventory, payment, shipping and the reconciler.

roles.label: State
roles.description: Carts, stock and holds, orders with the outbox, and the hot counter.

quiz.question: A shop runs checkout as one database transaction: read the stock, create the order, call the payment provider, decrement the stock, commit. In a sale, two shoppers both read 'stock = 1' and both orders are confirmed, and the payment call keeps row locks open for seconds. What is the best fix?
options: Lock the stock row for the whole transaction and raise the lock timeout, so the second shopper waits until the first order and its payment call have finished.
Reserve with one conditional update (decrement only where available is at least 1) that also writes an expiring hold, and call the payment provider after that transaction commits.
Decrement the stock as soon as an item enters the cart, with no expiry, so the unit is already taken before the shopper presses Buy and no read is needed at checkout.
Read the stock a second time just before the commit and abort the order if the value has changed, which closes the window between checking and decrementing.
quiz.explanation: The conditional update checks and decrements in one atomic step, so stock cannot go below zero, and the hold expires if the shopper never pays. The long lock only makes the payment wait worse, and a second read still leaves a gap between the read and the write. Taking stock at the cart locks units for abandoned carts.

quiz.question: A flash sale offers 20,000 units to 2 million shoppers who all press Buy in the same minute. Assume one stock row takes about 1,000 updates per second, so even one attempt each is over half an hour of queued updates, before any retries. What is the best way to protect the database?
options: Add application servers until all 2 million requests can run at once, so that no shopper waits for a free server and every request gets a connection.
Cache the stock count for 30 seconds on each application server, decrement the local copy and write the changes to the database in batches.
Shorten the hold expiry to 30 seconds, so units return quickly and more shoppers can be served in turn.
Put a waiting room at the edge that admits about as many shoppers as there are free units, and answer 'sold out' from an in-memory counter.
quiz.explanation: The bottleneck is lock contention on one row, so the fix is to keep most shoppers away from it. More servers just add more waiters, and local cached counts can sell the same unit on many servers. A shorter hold returns units faster but does nothing for the 2 million attempts.

quiz.question: The order service charged a shopper's card, then crashed before it marked the order confirmed. The order saga had saved its state before the charge. When the service restarts, the 5-minute stock hold has expired and another shopper took the last unit. What should the system do?
options: Resume the saga from saved state, repeat the charge with the same idempotency key, try for a new hold, and refund if the unit is gone.
Roll back the database transaction that created the order, which also reverses the charge at the provider, and ask the shopper to press Buy again.
Mark the order failed and let the card authorisation lapse by itself after a few days, because refunds should always be a manual decision by support.
Confirm the order anyway and back-order the unit, because the shopper has already paid and the sale must not be lost while stock is chased.
quiz.explanation: A saga persists its state so it can resume, and the idempotency key makes the repeated charge safe. A refund is the compensation when the unit cannot be re-reserved. A database rollback cannot undo money that already moved at the provider, and back-ordering is only valid if the shop can really supply the unit later.
